'''Robert Thomas Sauer''' (born 13 July 1948) is an American [[biochemist]] who is the [[Salvador E. Luria]] Professor of Biology at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].

==Early life and education==
Bob Sauer was born in [[Cornwall, New York]], in the [[Hudson Valley]] area of [[New York (state)|New York]]. He attended [[Amherst College]] in Massachusetts as an undergraduate and earned his bachelor's degree in [[biophysics]] in 1972. He received his PhD in [[Biochemistry]] and [[Molecular Biology]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1979.<ref name="hill_2009">{{cite journal |last1=Hill |first1=Robert L. |last2=Simoni |first2=Robert D. |last3=Kresge |first3=Nicole |title=A Model for Protein Turnover: the Work of Robert T. Sauer |journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry |date=4 December 2009 |volume=284 |issue=49 |pages=e22–e23 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(20)37726-7 |language=en |issn=0021-9258 |doi-access=free |pmc=2797215 }}</ref><ref name="cv">{{cite web |title=Robert T. Sauer Curriculum Vitae |url=http://web.mit.edu/sauerlab/new/rts-cv/bobs%20cv-2016.pdf |website=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |accessdate=20 January 2019}}</ref>

==Academic career==
Sauer joined the faculty at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1978, a year before he completed his PhD. He has remained at MIT for his entire academic career, becoming a [[full professor]] in 1987 and the [[Edwin C. Whitehead]] Professor in 1991. Sauer assumed his current appointment as the [[Salvador E. Luria]] Professor of Biology in 1999. He has held a number of service roles at MIT and spent five years, from 1999 to 2004, as the head of the biology department. He was the president of the [[Protein Society]] from 1997 to 1999.<ref name=hill_2009 /><ref name=cv />

Sauer was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1996 and to both the [[American Academy of Microbiology]] and the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in 1996.<ref name=hill_2009 /><ref name=cv /><ref name="nas">{{cite web |title=Robert Sauer |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/robert-t-sauer-hjw4hy/ |website=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=20 January 2019}}</ref> He has received both the [[Hans Neurath]] Award and the [[William Howard Stein|Stein]] and [[Stanford Moore|Moore]] Award from the Protein Society.<ref name=cv /><ref name="ps">{{cite web |title=Protein Society Awards |url=https://www.proteinsociety.org/page/protein-society-awards |website=The Protein Society |accessdate=20 January 2019 |archive-date=3 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191203162612/https://www.proteinsociety.org/page/protein-society-awards |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Research==
Sauer's research group has focused on [[protein structure]] and [[protein folding|folding]], and the relationship of structure to the molecular mechanisms of [[intermolecular interaction]]s such as [[DNA-binding protein|DNA binding]].<ref name=nas /><ref name="mitbio">{{cite web |title=Robert T. Sauer |url=https://biology.mit.edu/profile/robert-t-sauer/ |website=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |accessdate=20 January 2019}}</ref> His group has made significant contributions to the study of [[protein degradation]] and its regulation in living cells.<ref name=hill_2009 />
